morning24.text: Morning, {called}. Six months in Dr. Rao's office. You've kicked that door open four hundred and twelve times. I keep count.

then.text: The count rule's on every theatre wall. Not one swab left behind since. Neha laminated it, then laminated a spare.

else.text: Mr. Malhotra framed your photo for the corridor. It's next to the fire exit. Make of that what you will.

morning24.text: News from the top floor. Dean Menon retires at the end of the month. He's been Chief of Medicine since before the lifts worked.
The board votes for the next one on Friday. Your name's on the list. Mine isn't. I asked them to take it off; I'd rather teach than sit in meetings.
The other name is Dr. Sameer Kapoor. Medical Director of CarePlus Hospitals. Mr. Malhotra found him. He's touring the wards today.
And there's this. The union voted last night. Ninety-one percent. If the board won't move on pay and staffing, the nurses walk out on Thursday at eight.

then.text: You told the board you were on the nurses' side. I was in the corridor. I heard. Now's when that costs something.
You told the board you'd find the money they're pretending they don't have. That was six months ago. Did you find it?

else.text: You told the board a department lives within its budget. This department is living on Priya's double shifts.

choose.text: Then I'm with you. I'll write to the board today and say so, with my name on it.

then.text: In writing. Dr. Rao never put anything in writing.
then.head: tilt

then.text: ...Thank you. They'll still say no. But they'll have to say it to you.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Give me until Wednesday night. I'll take your numbers to the board myself and come back with an offer.

then.text: Wednesday night. If you come back with nothing, we walk. Nobody wants to. Everybody's tired.

choose.text: Call it off, Grace. If the nurses walk out, patients get hurt, and that's on the union.

then.text: Patients get hurt every night we're two nurses short. You just don't see it, because you go home.

morning24.text: Either way, the sickest keep their nurses. Life and limb cover. We plan it together on Thursday at seven, before I walk out. We're nurses, not monsters.
Dr. Kapoor's in admissions. Be polite. Then be yourself.
Mr. Malhotra: Dr. Kapoor is in the admissions bay. Could the Head of Department join us? Smile, please.

kapoor_tour.text: {called}, Dr. Sameer Kapoor. Medical Director of CarePlus. Twelve hospitals, four cities.
Fourteen, since Tuesday. Lovely ward. Very... authentic. Paper charts! My grandfather would weep.
At CarePlus a gallbladder is a day case. In at seven, home by six. Your average is two nights. That's a hotel, not a hospital.
Dr. Sethi started our day-case pilot on Tuesday. Dr. Kapoor's model. Three gallbladders, all home by evening.

choose.text: And how many of your day cases come back?

then.text: Come back? To us? Hardly any.
Where they go afterwards isn't really our department.
Ahem. Moving on.

choose.text: Some go home the same day. The ones who can. The rest stay until they're safe.

then.text: 'Safe.' A lovely word. Very hard to put on a spreadsheet.

choose.text: Welcome. Ask the nurses anything. They know this place better than I do.

then.text: I prefer numbers to stories. But thank you.
then.head: nod

kapoor_tour.text: I hear your nurses are threatening to strike. At CarePlus we use agency staff. Nobody strikes when nobody's permanent.
Friday, then. May the best manager win.
He has a very good tailor. And twelve slides on outsourcing. Fourteen, since Tuesday.

morning25.text: Emergency sent one up at five. Mrs. Rekha Sinha, fifty-two. Dr. Sethi took her gallbladder out on Saturday. The day-case pilot. Home by six.
Fever, and her belly's tight. Dr. Sethi's in clinic all morning, then the board's lunch for Dr. Kapoor.
She's yours, Head of Department. Go and see her before anyone decides what she's got.
Priya: Admissions. Mrs. Sinha. Thirty-nine degrees and a belly like a board. She's correcting my grammar.

sinha_arrive.text: Mrs. Sinha. Temperature thirty-nine, pulse a hundred and ten. Pressure's holding, for now.
Doctor. I taught Hindi for thirty-one years. I know the difference between 'some pain' and this.
The leaflet said some pain is normal. I waited two days, because of a leaflet. Ask me what you need to ask.

then.text: Three days after a keyhole gallbladder: pain spreading, fever, and she's yellowing. The scan shows fluid round her liver. A litre at least.

else.text: You missed some of it. Three days after her operation, pain spreading, and a fever. The scan shows fluid round her liver. A litre at least.

sinha_after.text: That's bile, until it proves otherwise. Something's leaking. She needs a look inside today, not after the board's lunch.

then.text: And the penicillin. Good that you asked. The day-case form says 'none known'. Somebody was in a hurry on Saturday.

sinha_after.text: Inside again? He said 'textbook'. Dr. Sethi. He said it twice, and then he ran. He had a conference. With slides.

choose.text: Something is leaking, probably bile, where your gallbladder was. We'll go back in through the same holes, wash it out and close it off.

then.text: Same holes. Good. I'd hate to waste them.
then.head: nod

choose.text: It's a known complication. We'll sort it out this afternoon.

then.text: 'A known complication.' Known to whom, Doctor? Not to me.

sinha_after.text: Priya: Theatre 2 at two o'clock for Mrs. Sinha. Dr. Sethi's clinic says he's 'unavailable'.

sinha_ready.text: My son is driving from Lucknow. He's a lawyer. Please be finished before he arrives; he asks questions in paragraphs.
And, Doctor. Whatever you find. Tell me the whole sentence, not half of it.
sinha_ready.head: tilt

bile_brief.text: Your patient, your lead. I'll hold the camera and keep my opinions under the drapes.
Neha. Three ports, a clip applier loaded with six, and a drain on the side, just in case. Everything on the board.
Fifty-two, septic, and there's a penicillin allergy somewhere in her history, depending on whose form you believe. I'll go gently.
Time-out, Doctor. I'll read the board.

then.text: She's washed out and the leak's dealt with. I finished it. Septic patients don't give you time. Learn it; don't carry it.
Washed out and dry. She'll feel better by tonight than she has all week.
then.head: nod

else.text: Messier than it needed to be. But she's washed out, and the leak's dealt with.

then.text: And she reacted to the co-amoxiclav. Penicillin, like she told Saturday's form. Dr. Khan caught it. Read the allergy before you confirm it.
One clip on the stump, and one lying loose in her belly. Dr. Sethi's notes say 'two clips applied, secure'.
One of them was never on properly. He was rushing. Six cases on a pilot list, and a train to a conference at seven.
then.head: down

then.text: A little duct straight out of the liver bed. One person in a hundred has one. Nobody's fault.
But she was home by six on Saturday, with a leaflet that told her pain was normal, and nobody rang her. That part's somebody's fault.
A burn on the side of her main duct. The hook, too close, too fast. The liver team stents it in the morning; she should heal without another operation.
It happens to good surgeons. It happens more to good surgeons in a hurry.
then.head: down

sinha_after_op.text: Dr. Sethi's at the desk. He's heard. He'd like a word with the Head of Department.

sethi_leak.text: I've read the op note. Mine, and yours.

then.text: I wrote two clips. I believed it when I wrote it. I was thinking about the slides.
then.head: down

then.text: A burn on the main duct. I've never... I've done four hundred of these.
A duct in the liver bed. Nobody could have seen it. It's in every textbook as a known complication.

sethi_leak.text: The board votes on Friday. Kapoor's pitch is that we're careless and slow. If this is on the incident list before Friday, it's his whole presentation.
I'm not asking for me. Well. Not only for me. Wait until Monday. Then I'll tell her everything, I promise. Just not this week.

choose.text: No. You tell her today, and I'll stand beside you. Then we both write it up.

then.text: Side by side. Like you did for Dr. Rao.
then.head: nod

then.text: He told me about that. He said it was the worst hour of his life, and the best thing anyone did for him.
then.head: down

choose.text: She's told today. By you, if you'll do it. By me, if you won't. And it goes on the list today too.

then.text: ...I'll do it. You don't have to come. I'd rather you didn't watch.

choose.text: Monday, then. After the vote. But Monday, Kabir. Not Tuesday.

then.text: Monday. Thank you.
then.head: nod

then.text: Mrs. Sinha asked for the whole sentence, {called}. Not half of it.

choose.text: Write it up as a known complication. It happens. Nobody needs a hearing about it.

then.text: A known complication. Yes. It is one. Mostly.
then.head: down

then.text: I'll pretend I didn't hear that, {called}. I'm not good at pretending.
Priya: Mrs. Sinha's awake. Asking for 'the doctor with the whole sentence'. And Dr. Sethi.
Doctor. And Dr. Sethi, who said 'textbook'.
Mrs. Sinha. On Saturday I put a clip on the duct from your gallbladder. I wrote that I'd put two. I hadn't. The one that was there slipped, and bile leaked into your belly.
Mrs. Sinha. On Saturday, working too fast, I burnt the side of your main bile duct. It leaked. The liver team will put a small tube inside it tomorrow, so it heals.
Mrs. Sinha. A tiny duct in your liver was leaking. That can happen to anyone. But I sent you home six hours after the operation, and nobody rang you. That part's on me.
And you stood there the whole time. Like a bookend.
then.head: tilt

then.text: Thirty-one years of girls telling me the dog ate their homework. You know which ones I liked? The ones who said 'I didn't do it, Ma'am. I'm sorry.'
Full sentence, Doctor. Subject, verb, sorry. Well done.
then.head: nod

then.text: ...Thank you, Ma'am.
then.head: down

else.text: Dr. Sethi was here an hour ago. On his own. He stood where you're standing and told me himself.

then.text: A clip he wrote down and never put on properly. He said it three times, as if once wasn't enough.
A burn on a duct, because he was hurrying. A little tube tomorrow, he says, and no more operations.
A little duct, nobody's fault, he said. And a leaflet that should have been a phone call. That was his fault, he said.

else.text: Thirty-one years of girls telling me the dog ate their homework. The ones I liked said 'I didn't do it, Ma'am. I'm sorry.' He said it properly. Subject, verb, sorry.

choose.text: And the day-case pilot stops until every patient gets a phone call the next morning. I'll sign that tonight.

then.text: A phone call. Imagine. My son will be so disappointed; he'd prepared paragraphs.

choose.text: Is there anything you want to ask us?

then.text: Only one thing. Will the next Mrs. Sinha get a phone call?
then.head: tilt

then.text: Yes. I'll make sure of it.

strike_rota_arrive.text: Seven o'clock. I'm in my own clothes, and that placard is face down because I can't bear to look at it.

then.text: You took our numbers to the board on Wednesday. They offered a review in six months. Six months is a very long time on nights.
Your letter was read out at the union meeting. They clapped. Then the board didn't answer it, and they voted to walk anyway.

else.text: You asked me to call it off. I asked the members. Ninety-four percent, this time. You helped.

strike_rota_arrive.text: Life and limb cover. Priya, Tom from theatres, an agency nurse who started yesterday, and whoever else I could beg. They stay. Everyone else walks at eight.
Every patient gets a name next to them. Nobody carries more than they can. Do it with me. Then I go.

then.text: That's a rota I'd sign on a good day. Everybody covered, nobody drowning.
then.head: nod

then.text: Somebody had no name next to them, Doctor. I've fixed it. Don't make me come back in from the gate.

else.text: It'll hold, mostly. But someone's carrying more than they should. Watch them at midday.

strike_rota_after.text: Priya has my number. If anyone's dying, I come back in, strike or no strike. Everyone knows that. Even the board.

strike_midday.text: Midday report, Head of Department. It's very quiet. Quiet the wrong way.

then.text: Everyone's had their checks on time. Tom says theatre nursing is easier; at least in theatre the patients don't ask for tea.
A drip ran dry for two hours. The agency nurse saw it but isn't allowed to touch IV here, and I was on the other side of the floor.
A confused patient climbed out of bed and fell. A bruise, nothing broken. His nurse had too many to watch.
Infection control found the same nurse going from the infected wound to the chemo patient. They've swabbed everybody. Twice.
Somebody's two o'clock checks happened at four. Nothing bad happened. This time.
then.head: down

then.text: Ananya had the heaviest patient on the floor. She did well. She also cried in the sluice.

strike_midday.text: Ah, {called}. Good news. Dr. Kapoor has offered us CarePlus agency nurses. Twelve of them, here by four o'clock. All you need to do is sign.
Agency nurses through the picket line. On the day.

choose.text: No. We don't bring people in through the picket line. We'll cover it ourselves, and I'll ask the board for a real offer today.

then.text: The board will hear about this.
Good. I'll tell them myself.

choose.text: Sign it. Patients come before principles today.

then.text: Patients come before principles. Write that on my placard, Doctor.
Four o'clock. I'll have them sign in at the side door.

strike_midday.text: Priya: Grace says the picket's come in out of the rain, to admissions. She says bring tea, if you're coming. Or don't come.

picket.text: Head of Department. On the picket line. We brought it in out of the rain; admissions is technically outside the ward. Mr. Malhotra will need a lie down.

then.text: Twelve agency nurses went in by the side door at four. Kapoor's. Everyone on this line saw them.
They'll go home tonight, and so will we. The strike's over, because you broke it. The board won't need to offer us anything now.
then.head: down

else.text: Priya says you sent the agency back. Nobody on this line will forget that.
else.head: nod

else.text: Nor will the board.
Mrs. Rajan came down at four. On foot. She's been standing here an hour, listening.
Two more nurses on every night shift from the first of the month, and a pay review in March. With the union at the table, and the Head of Department beside me.
...We'll put it to the members tonight. It'll pass.

choose.text: I brought tea. Eleven cups. I counted the placards.

then.text: Eleven. You counted us. That's the most Head-of-Department thing you've ever done.

choose.text: Thank you for leaving us cover. You came back for the man who fell. I saw.

then.text: Of course I came back. I'm on strike, not dead.
We're back. The agency nurses left at seven. One of them took a stapler. Nobody's offered us anything.

else.text: We're back. Two more nurses on nights from the first. Priya cried. If you tell her I told you, I'll deny it under oath.

morning27.text: Board at three. Dr. Kapoor's been here since seven with a man carrying a projector. He's practising his pauses.

then.text: And Mrs. Sinha's son arrived last night. The lawyer. He's asked for every page of her notes. And the operation videos. Both of them.

morning27.text: Answer what they ask. Say 'I don't know' when you don't. And don't try to out-slide Kapoor. Nobody can.
Priya: Mrs. Sinha's going home today. She'd like to see you first. She says it's about grammar.

then.text: Going home. With a phone number, and a nurse who's going to ring me tomorrow at nine. I've written it in my diary. In ink.
Dr. Sethi came back last night and sat with me for an hour. He's frightened of you, you know. In the good way.
then.head: tilt

else.text: Going home. My son says I should ask you something directly, so I will.
Why was I in theatre twice, Doctor? Whole sentence, please.

choose.text: Something went wrong in your first operation, and it was ours, not bad luck. Dr. Sethi wants to tell you himself, and he will, today. I'm sorry we waited.

then.text: You waited for your vote. I'm not a fool, Doctor. But you told me before it. That counts. A little.
then.head: nod

choose.text: A known complication. It happens, even with the best surgeons.

then.text: 'Known.' That word again. My son will be pleased. He likes it when people use that word.

else.text: A known complication, they wrote. My son has a different word for it. Several, actually.

board_vote.text: We've heard Dr. Kapoor. Forty minutes, three videos and a pause that lasted longer than my marriage. Now you.
First question. On Thursday the nurses walked out. Tell me what you did.

then.text: I'll answer that. CarePlus supplied twelve nurses at a day's notice. The strike ended by evening. Efficiency.

choose.text: I signed for the agency nurses. It kept the ward safe for an afternoon, and it cost me the nurses' trust. I'd want that trust back before I ran anything bigger.

then.text: Honest. Expensive, but honest.
then.head: nod

choose.text: I kept the ward running. That's the job.

then.text: The ward is the nurses. You'll find that out.

else.text: I know what you did. I was on the picket line. I'd like you to say it anyway, for the minutes.

choose.text: Grace built the cover rota with me before she walked out. We kept the sickest safe, sent the agency back, and you came down and made an offer.

then.text: And I'd like the minutes to say the Head of Department stood on a picket line with eleven cups of tea.
then.head: nod

else.text: Grace said you'd give her the credit. She asked me to minute that she accepts it.
else.head: nod

choose.text: I planned the cover, refused the agency, and asked you to come down. If it had gone wrong, it was mine.

then.text: It didn't go wrong. Noted.
then.head: nod

then.text: One small thing. I've read the midday report from Thursday. The cover wasn't perfect.
No. It wasn't. I'll plan it better, and I'll plan it with more nurses.

board_vote.text: My question, Chair, if I may. Mrs. Rekha Sinha. A day case in this department, back three days later with bile in her belly.

then.text: Her son sent me the operation videos, and the discharge letter. 'Known complication', the letter says. Signed by the Head of Department. The videos say something longer.
Is that true?

choose.text: Yes. Dr. Sethi asked me to keep it quiet until after this meeting, and I agreed. It was wrong. I'll tell her myself today, and I'm sorry.

then.text: You learned this lesson six months ago, with Mrs. Kurup. Apparently it didn't stick.

else.text: Mrs. Kurup's lawyer is on my desk as well. This is becoming a habit, Doctor. Break it.

choose.text: Bile leaks are a known complication. The letter wasn't false.

then.text: Not false. Just not true. I've heard that one before. I gave it up in 1998.
then.head: shake

then.text: She was told this morning, I believe. Three days late. Better than never. Not as good as Tuesday.

else.text: I've read the incident report. Filed on the day, with the surgeon's name on it. And she was told the same afternoon, by the surgeon.

then.text: And the day-case pilot is paused until every patient gets a phone call the next morning. Signed by the Head of Department.
Paused? Day cases are the future.
Then the future can wait for a phone call.

else.text: Dr. Kapoor, how do CarePlus patients learn about their complications?
else.head: tilt

else.text: We... track readmissions very closely. To our own hospitals.

board_vote.text: Last question. Mine. I've been Chief of Medicine for nineteen years. What is a Chief of Medicine for?
board_vote.head: tilt

choose.text: Making sure nobody is ever alone on a shift. Doctor or nurse. Everything else follows.

then.text: I said that once, at my first board meeting. Then I forgot it for nineteen years.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Making sure every patient gets the whole sentence. What we did, what went wrong, what happens next.

then.text: The whole sentence. Mrs. Sinha's phrase. She wrote to me too.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Making the next lot better than us. Every junior, every nurse, every intern.

then.text: Meera Iyer will be insufferable.

choose.text: Keeping the hospital solvent. Nothing else works if the lights go out.

then.text: Finally. Somebody gets it.
The lights are Mr. Malhotra's job. The people are yours.

board_vote.text: Thank you both. We've voted while Dr. Kapoor was setting up his projector. He took a while.

then.text: Four votes to three. Mine decided it, and I very nearly didn't cast it.
Five votes to two.
then.head: nod

else.text: Six votes to one. Mr. Malhotra would like it minuted that he voted for the other candidate. Loudly.

board_vote.text: Congratulations. Genuinely. If you ever want twelve hospitals, call me. Fourteen.
My office is on the top floor. The window opens if you swear at it. Use it often; the view helps.
Your first budget meeting is Monday at eight. I'll bring a brochure. Two, now.

morning28.text: Chief. I'm going to have to practise that. Chief.
Rajan wants a name for Head of Surgery by tonight. Your old office. The door that sticks.

choose.text: You. You've been running this department from the lightbox for years.

then.text: I said no to the board. I'll say yes to you. On one condition: I keep teaching on Tuesdays, and nobody schedules a meeting on a Tuesday.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Kabir. He told Mrs. Sinha the truth himself. That's the one thing a head of department can't learn from a course.

then.text: Kabir. Who'd have thought. He'll put the parking space in the job description.

choose.text: Advertise it, properly. Everyone applies, and the best one gets it.

then.text: Very fair. Very slow. Grace will run it in the meantime and nobody will notice the difference.

morning28.text: And your new intern is here. First day. She's been in the corridor since six, reading the fire notices.
Go on. You've waited years to do this to somebody.

intern_day1.text: Dr. Ira Saxena. Intern. Sorry, I'm early. I've read every fire notice twice. There are four exits and a hose.
Morning, Dr. Saxena. Handover. Pen out.
Pen. Yes. I have three. In case.
Bed one: Mr. Ghosh, hernia, going home today. He's been going home since Thursday. He'll tell you about his son. Twice. Bed four: Mrs. Sinha's bed, clean sheets, waiting for whoever comes next.
Can I ask something? What do I do first? Honestly?
intern_day1.head: tilt

choose.text: Ask, whenever you don't know. Every single time. Nobody here minds. The ones who don't ask are the ones we worry about.

then.text: Every time. Even the stupid ones?
then.head: tilt

then.text: Especially those. They're the ones that kill people.

choose.text: Be more scared of the families than the surgery. Then go and talk to them anyway.

then.text: Somebody said that to me once, on their first day. I told them the ones who aren't scared don't last.

choose.text: Read the notes, wash your hands, and never sign a count you didn't finish yourself.

then.text: That's on the poster in theatre. The laminated one.
Neha laminated a spare.

intern_day1.text: Where every round starts. With the patient you know. Bed one.
I don't know any patients yet.
You will by lunchtime. Off you go. Don't run.

ending.text: Do you remember your first operation? Rohit's appendix. You held the scalpel like a pen and apologised to it.
Rohit sent a card last week. He builds bridges now. His mother still rings him twice a day. Once to ask if the bridges are safe.

then.text: Mrs. Kurup writes every month. Four pages about her garden, one line about you. This month's line was 'Tell the young surgeon I'm still not dead. Thanks to them.'

else.text: Mrs. Kurup's lawyer writes every month. Mrs. Kurup doesn't.
else.head: down

then.text: Zoya's a registrar in Pune now. She's very good. She's never rung.
then.head: down

else.text: Zoya came first in the state exams. She told the examiners she reads a drug chart like a crime scene, and that you taught her.
else.head: nod

ending.text: Dr. Rao grows roses in Coorg. He sent a photo. The moustache has gone completely grey. The roses are very red.

then.text: And Kabir's moved into your old office. He kicked the door on the right. It didn't open. He's been in there an hour.
And I've moved into your old office. I kicked the door on the left, like Dr. Rao said. It opened. I nearly cried.
Still one nurse short on nights. Still counting. But I'll forgive you eventually. Probably at your retirement.

else.text: And the two new night nurses start on the first. I'm going to terrify them. Lovingly.

ending.text: From intern to Chief of Medicine, {called}. Do you know what's changed?
ending.head: tilt

choose.text: Nothing important. The pager still goes off. I still answer it.

then.text: Good answer. The ones who stop answering are the ones who stop being doctors.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Everything. I used to be scared of getting it wrong. Now I'm scared of other people being too scared to tell me when I do.

then.text: That took me twenty years. Don't tell anyone you got there faster.

choose.text: You. You never put your hands over mine. Even when you wanted to.

then.text: I always wanted to. Every single time.

ending.text: It's half past six, Chief. Go home.
